body:
Why Plants Have Different Carbon-Fixation Pathways

Photosynthesis requires carbon dioxide, but obtaining carbon dioxide creates a difficulty for terrestrial plants. When stomata open to admit atmospheric carbon dioxide, water vapour can escape from the leaves.

Different plants have evolved different ways to manage carbon fixation and water conservation. Three important pathways are known as C3, C4 and CAM.

All 3 ultimately use the Calvin cycle to manufacture carbohydrates. Their main differences concern the initial handling of carbon dioxide and the organisation of carbon fixation.

C3 Photosynthesis

In C3 plants, carbon dioxide enters the Calvin cycle directly. The first stable product formed through the initial carbon-fixation reaction is a compound containing 3 carbon atoms, called 3-phosphoglyceric acid or 3-PGA.

This 3-carbon product gives the pathway its name.

Wheat, rice, soybean and cotton are familiar examples of C3 crops.

C3 photosynthesis works well under many ordinary growing conditions. However, under hot conditions, especially when carbon dioxide inside the leaf becomes limited, a process called photorespiration can reduce photosynthetic efficiency.

Photorespiration is associated with an oxygen-consuming activity of the carbon-fixing enzyme RuBisCO. The detailed biochemical pathway is not necessary for the basic distinction between C3 and C4 plants.

C4 Photosynthesis

In C4 plants, carbon dioxide is initially incorporated into a compound containing 4 carbon atoms. The first stable product is oxaloacetic acid, commonly abbreviated OAA.

Carbon dioxide is first fixed in mesophyll cells. Carbon-containing compounds then move to specialised bundle-sheath cells, where carbon dioxide is released and enters the Calvin cycle.

This separation of initial carbon fixation and the Calvin cycle between different cell types is called spatial separation.

Many C4 plants have a characteristic arrangement of prominent bundle-sheath cells around vascular bundles called Kranz anatomy.

Maize, sorghum, sugarcane and pearl millet are C4 plants. Sorghum and pearl millet are also familiar dryland crops in western India.

C4 photosynthesis is advantageous in many warm, sunny environments because its carbon-concentrating mechanism greatly reduces photorespiration. However, this does not mean every plant growing in a hot region must be a C4 plant.

CAM Photosynthesis

CAM stands for Crassulacean Acid Metabolism. It occurs in many plants adapted to environments where conserving water is particularly important.

In a typical CAM plant, stomata open mainly at night, when the air is usually cooler and evaporation losses are lower. Carbon dioxide enters the leaf and is temporarily stored in the form of organic acids, commonly including malic acid.

During daylight, the stomata generally remain closed or less open. The stored organic acids release carbon dioxide inside photosynthetic cells, allowing the Calvin cycle to use it while reducing water loss.

The initial capture of carbon dioxide and its later use are separated mainly by time rather than by different cell types.

Cacti, pineapple and several other succulent plants are familiar examples of CAM photosynthesis.

CAM plants do not ordinarily manufacture all their food at night. They mainly collect and store carbon dioxide at night, then use the stored carbon dioxide for photosynthetic carbohydrate production during the day.

Comparison of the Three Pathways

FeatureC3C4CAM
Initial stable carbon-fixation product3-carbon 3-PGA4-carbon OAA4-carbon organic compounds formed at night
OrganisationDirect Calvin-cycle fixationSpatial separation between mesophyll and bundle-sheath cellsTemporal separation between night and day
Typical stomatal openingMainly during daylightMainly during daylightMainly during night
Important advantageEffective under many moderate conditionsReduced photorespiration under warm, bright conditionsReduced water loss in dry environments
ExamplesWheat, riceMaize, sorghumCactus, pineapple

The Central Distinction

The difference between the pathways is not that only C3 plants perform the Calvin cycle. The Calvin cycle is common to C3, C4 and CAM photosynthesis.

C3 plants fix carbon dioxide directly through the Calvin cycle. C4 plants first concentrate carbon dioxide using reactions organised between different leaf cell types. CAM plants collect carbon dioxide mainly at night and release it for use during the day.

Environmental conditions influence which pathway offers an advantage, but the pathway used by a plant is a biological characteristic of that species, not a daily choice made by every plant.

Prelims focus

  • C3 refers to the 3-carbon first stable product, 3-PGA.
  • C4 refers to the 4-carbon first stable product, OAA.
  • C4 plants commonly show Kranz anatomy and spatial separation of carbon fixation.
  • CAM plants commonly open stomata at night to conserve water.
  • Wheat and rice are C3 crops; maize and sorghum are C4 crops.
  • Trap: CAM plants store carbon dioxide at night; the Calvin cycle uses the stored carbon during the day.

[Sources: NCERT, Biology, Class 11, Chapter 11, Photosynthesis in Higher Plants, Sections 11.7–11.9, printed pp. 142–149, reprint 2026–27; NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 5, Life Processes, Section 5.2.1, printed p. 82, reprint 2026–27; CBSE, Introductory Agriculture, Class 9, classification of crops by photosynthetic pathway; Khan Academy, C3, C4, and CAM Plants, sections comparing carbon fixation and CAM plants, consulted 4 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Many cacti survive in dry habitats using water-conserving adaptations, including CAM photosynthesis.

title: C3, C4 and CAM Photosynthesis: Basic Differences and Examples

body:
What Are Stomata?

Stomata are microscopic pores found in the epidermis of leaves and some other green plant parts. Each pore is called a stoma.

In typical leaves, a stomatal pore is bordered by 2 specialised cells called guard cells. These cells regulate the opening and closing of the pore.

Stomata are particularly important because they provide a route for gas exchange while also allowing water vapour to escape.

How Guard Cells Control Stomata

Guard cells change shape according to their water content.

  • Opening: When guard cells take up water and become turgid, their shape changes and the stomatal pore opens.
  • Closing: When guard cells lose water and become less turgid, the pore narrows or closes.

This regulation helps the plant balance its requirement for carbon dioxide against the risk of excessive water loss.

The Two Main Functions of Stomata

Gas Exchange

During photosynthesis, carbon dioxide generally diffuses from the atmosphere into leaves through open stomata. Oxygen produced during photosynthesis can diffuse outward.

Stomata also permit the movement of respiratory gases. However, gaseous exchange in plants is not restricted entirely to stomata; other plant surfaces also participate.

Water-Vapour Loss

When stomata are open, water vapour can escape from the moist internal surfaces of the leaf into the atmosphere.

This water loss is a major component of transpiration.

Transpiration is the loss of water in the form of vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, particularly through stomata in leaves.

Water evaporates from moist cell surfaces inside the leaf and diffuses outward as vapour. A smaller amount can also be lost through the cuticle, the protective surface covering of leaves.

Why Transpiration Is Useful

Although transpiration involves water loss, it performs important functions when the plant has an adequate water supply.

Assisting the Upward Movement of Water

As water evaporates from leaf tissues, it creates a pulling force on the continuous column of water in the xylem. This is called transpiration pull.

Transpiration pull helps move water and dissolved mineral nutrients from roots towards the upper parts of the plant.

Cooling the Plant

Evaporation removes heat from leaf surfaces. Transpiration therefore contributes to temperature regulation, particularly when plants are exposed to sunlight.

Factors Affecting Transpiration

The rate of transpiration depends on both environmental conditions and the opening of stomata.

FactorUsual effect when other conditions are suitable
Higher temperatureOften increases evaporation and water-vapour loss
Higher atmospheric humidityUsually reduces transpiration
Higher wind speedOften increases transpiration by removing moist air near leaves
Greater light availabilityOften increases stomatal opening in ordinary daytime-opening plants
Low soil-water availabilityCan cause stomatal closure and reduce transpiration

These relationships describe general tendencies, not unconditional rules. Extremely hot or dry conditions can make a plant close its stomata, reducing transpiration even when temperature is high.

High temperature does not always produce high transpiration. If water becomes insufficient, stomatal closure may restrict water loss.

Stomatal Behaviour During Day and Night

In many ordinary C3 and C4 plants, stomata tend to open during daylight, when photosynthesis requires carbon dioxide, and close during darkness.

CAM plants illustrate an important exception. Their stomata commonly open at night, allowing carbon dioxide uptake with reduced water loss. The stored carbon dioxide can then be used during the following day.

Adaptations That Reduce Water Loss

Plants growing in dry habitats may possess thick waxy cuticles, reduced leaves, spines or specialised stomatal behaviour. In some cacti, green stems perform photosynthesis while leaves are reduced to spines.

Such features can reduce water loss, but their effectiveness depends on the plant and its environment.

Connection Between Transpiration and Photosynthesis

Photosynthesis benefits from open stomata because carbon dioxide can enter. Transpiration also generally increases when stomata are open because water vapour escapes through the same pores.

During water shortage, closing stomata helps conserve water but also reduces the availability of carbon dioxide for photosynthesis. This is a fundamental relationship in plant physiology.

Prelims focus

  • Stomata are pores involved in gas exchange and transpiration.
  • Guard cells regulate stomatal opening and closing.
  • Turgid guard cells generally open a stomatal pore.
  • Transpiration is the loss of water as vapour from aerial plant parts.
  • Transpiration helps water movement and leaf cooling.
  • Trap: Most ordinary plants open stomata mainly during daylight, but CAM plants commonly open them at night.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 5, Life Processes, Section 5.2.1 and Figure 5.3, printed pp. 83–84, and Section 5.4.2, printed pp. 94–95, reprint 2026–27; NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 11, Transportation in Animals and Plants, Transpiration, printed p. 130, 2018–19 reprint; OpenStax, Biology 2e, Section 30.5, Control of Transpiration; Food and Agriculture Organization, FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56, Chapter 1, Evaporation and Transpiration, consulted 4 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Changes in guard-cell water content regulate stomatal opening and closing.

title: Stomata, Guard Cells and Transpiration in Plants

body:
Why Plants Need an Internal Transport System

Photosynthesis occurs mainly in green aerial tissues, but terrestrial plants obtain most water and mineral nutrients from the soil. Water absorbed by roots may have to travel a considerable distance before reaching leaves.

In small structures, substances can move over short distances through diffusion or osmosis. In larger plants, these processes alone cannot efficiently supply distant tissues.

Plants therefore possess specialised conducting tissues called xylem and phloem. Xylem is principally responsible for transporting water and dissolved mineral nutrients.

Absorption of Water by Roots

The Role of Root Hairs

Roots possess many fine projections called root hairs. They are extensions of individual epidermal cells and increase the surface area available for absorption from soil water.

Water generally enters root cells by osmosis, moving across selectively permeable cell membranes in response to differences in water potential.

At the school level, this can be understood as the movement of water from a region where water is more readily available to a region where it is less readily available across a selectively permeable membrane.

Absorption of Mineral Ions

Roots also absorb dissolved mineral ions. Some ions are taken up through energy-dependent transport processes.

The accumulation of mineral ions in root tissues can promote water entry by osmosis. Water and minerals subsequently enter the xylem for distribution to other parts of the plant.

Structure and Function of Xylem

Xylem is the vascular tissue primarily responsible for conducting water and dissolved mineral nutrients from roots to stems, leaves and other plant parts.

Xylem contains specialised water-conducting elements called vessels and tracheids. These form interconnected pathways through roots, stems and leaves.

In mature plants, xylem vessels and tracheids are generally dead cells with strengthened walls. Their structure allows water to pass through them and also contributes to mechanical support.

The main direction of xylem transport in a transpiring terrestrial plant is upward, from roots towards aerial tissues.

What Makes Water Rise in Xylem?

Root Pressure

When mineral ions accumulate in root tissues, water enters by osmosis and can generate positive pressure within the root xylem. This is called root pressure.

Root pressure can contribute to upward water movement, especially under conditions of low transpiration. Its contribution may be relatively important during the night in certain plants.

However, root pressure alone generally cannot explain the movement of water to the tops of tall trees.

Transpiration Pull

When water evaporates from the surfaces of leaf cells, water is drawn from nearby xylem vessels to replace it.

This creates tension in the xylem water column. The resulting upward pull is called transpiration pull.

Water molecules are attracted to one another, a property called cohesion. Their attraction to the walls of conducting tissues also helps maintain the water column.

Because xylem forms a continuous conducting system, tension generated near the leaves can pull water upwards from the roots.

Root Pressure and Transpiration Pull Compared

FeatureRoot pressureTranspiration pull
OriginWater entry associated with mineral accumulation in rootsEvaporation of water from leaves
Type of forcePositive pressureTension or suction
Typical importanceCan contribute during low transpirationMajor driving force in many actively transpiring plants
Importance in tall treesUsually insufficient by itselfPrincipal mechanism supporting upward water movement

Applying the Concept

A well-watered plant exposed to suitable sunlight can lose water through its leaves. Continued transpiration creates a pull that helps replace the lost water through xylem.

However, if soil water becomes insufficient, the roots cannot replace water at the required rate. Guard cells may lose turgor, stomata may close, and the plant may wilt. Stomatal closure reduces further water loss but also restricts carbon dioxide entry.

This illustrates how root absorption, xylem transport, transpiration and photosynthesis are functionally connected.

Prelims focus

  • Root hairs increase the surface area for water absorption.
  • Water enters root cells primarily by osmosis.
  • Xylem transports water and dissolved mineral nutrients.
  • Vessels and tracheids are water-conducting xylem elements.
  • Transpiration pull is the major force for upward water movement in many transpiring plants.
  • Trap: Root pressure may assist water transport but generally cannot independently account for water rising through tall trees.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 5, Life Processes, Section 5.4.2, Transport of Water, printed pp. 94–95, reprint 2026–27; GCERT, Science, Std. 10, Chapter 5, Life Processes, Section 5.4.2, printed pp. 94–95; NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 11, Transportation in Animals and Plants, Section 11.3, printed pp. 128–130, 2018–19 reprint; OpenStax, Biology 2e, Section 30.5, Movement of Water and Minerals in the Xylem, consulted 4 November 2026.]
